text: Stand to the right of a binary tree and look at it. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — what I can see means: for each depth, the node that sits furthest to the right at that depth. One node per level, top to bottom. Is that right?

Then let me say the trap out loud, because I think it is the whole problem. Rightmost at a depth is not the same as right child. If a node has no right child, its left subtree can still stick out further right than anything else at that depth. So the answer is one node per level, and which node it is depends only on its position within the level — not on whether it arrived as a left child or a right child.

One consequence I want to check with you. If the tree is a chain going only left, every level has exactly one node, so every node is visible. The right side view of a left-only chain is the entire chain. Does that match your definition?
Are there any constraints on the input size? And can the root be null?
Up to one hundred nodes, and yes, the root can be null. Return an empty list then.

Let me run through the example: one, two, three, null, five, null, four. Level one is just one. Level two is two and three, so I see three. Level three holds five and four — five is the right child of two, four is the right child of three. Four is last, so the answer is one, three, four. Notice that node five is a right child and still invisible. So being a right child clearly is not the rule.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to just follow the right pointers from the root and collect what I pass. It's two lines, and it's wrong. Across all six thousand nine hundred eighteen tree shapes up to nine nodes, it fails on six thousand five hundred fifty-five — ninety-four point seven five percent. It only works when the right spine is as long as the tree is tall. This problem reminds me of a plain level order traversal. If I already have the nodes grouped by level, in order, the answer is just the last item of each group. So I'll run BFS with a queue and keep one node per level.

Here's the plan. One: push the root. Two: at the top of each round, freeze the level width, size equals the queue's size. Three: pop that many nodes, push children left then right, and record the node where i equals size minus one — the last one at this depth. One thing worth flagging — size must be frozen before the inner loop, because I push children into the same queue I pop from. Against the live size, the last-of-level test fires on the wrong node and levels merge. There's a trade-off here. A right-first DFS that records the first node at each new depth uses a height-sized stack instead of a width-sized queue. I prefer BFS because the rule, last node at this depth, is stated directly in the code. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. A null root returns an empty list right away. Then it's standard BFS: freeze size, pop that many nodes, push the left child before the right, and record the value when i equals size minus one. One thing worth flagging — that test looks at nothing but queue position. It never asks whether u is a left or a right child, which is exactly the property I wanted, and it's why the left-only chain needs no special case. A nice sanity check: change the test to i equals zero, and the same code gives the left side view — the opposite end of the level.

Let's dry-run the code. One, two, three, null, five, null, four — expected one, three, four. The row that matters is level three: the queue holds five, then four. Five pops at i equals zero and is skipped, even though it's a right child, because its parent two sat left of three on the level above. Left-to-right order carries down, and position is all the test looks at. Four pops last and is recorded, so I get one, three, four. That matches. Corner cases: a null root returns an empty list at the guard. A single node returns just itself. A left-only chain of five nodes returns all five, the case the right-spine shortcut gets wrong. And the answer length always equals the tree height.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each node is pushed once and popped once, with constant work. Space is order of w, the widest level, and the output adds order of h. The worst case is a perfect tree: the bottom level holds about half the nodes, so the queue peaks near n over two. The DFS version flips this — its stack is worse on a chain and better on a wide tree. Oh, one more thing — this code never compares values; it only counts positions. So duplicates and negatives are fine, and a left view would be a one-line change.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You attacked the walk-the-right-spine instinct with a real measurement — ninety-four point seven five percent of shapes broken — and gave the exact condition under which it accidentally works. You used the example against yourself: node five is a right child and still invisible, which proves selection is about queue position. And you found a free invariant — answer length equals tree height. Good work.
